activities.anchor: Algorithm choice is a hardware decision, and it is free
activities.caption: call the work gap at a million items
activities.name: algChoiceEst

config.prompt: Both sorting methods finish on a million items — how many times more work does the n² method do?
config.why: n² = 10¹² against n log n ≈ 2×10⁷ — a factor near 50,000. At a billion items the gap is the difference between days and under a minute.
config.context: Same list, same machine — the only variable was the method.

activities.anchor: The design pipeline has four moves
activities.caption: problem to algorithm — put the pipeline in order
activities.name: algDesignOrder

config.prompt: From problem statement to typable program — put the pipeline in order:
items: Decompose: split the problem into subproblems you can state precisely
Specify: write each piece's inputs, output, and the relationship between them
Write pseudocode: structured English, every move unambiguous, no language syntax chosen yet
Refine: expand anything still fuzzy until it could be typed straight into a program
config.why: Cheap on paper, dear in code — the fuzziness dies before a language is chosen.

activities.anchor: Every element is there for a reason, and each reason is a place a bug could live.
activities.caption: pair each pattern with its memorised skeleton
activities.name: algPatternsMatch

config.prompt: Pair each standard pattern with its skeleton:

pairs.right: total ← 0 before the loop; total ← total + value inside
same shape, but count ← count + 1 only when a condition holds
start from the first item; replace the running best when a newcomer beats it

config.why: Five skeletons, five adapted variables — and the running best must start as a real item of the list, never a guess like 0.

activities.anchor: That is the phone book's trick, formalised.
activities.caption: how many halvings for a million items?
activities.name: algBinaryPlace

config.prompt: Binary search on a list of a million items — at most how many comparisons?
config.why: Each comparison halves the candidates: a million is about 2²⁰, so twenty halvings reach one item — 1,000 needs 10, a billion needs 30.

activities.anchor: binary search is always faster, so I should always sort first
activities.caption: one lookup today, ten thousand tomorrow — walk the trade
activities.name: algSearchBranch

config.root: One list, many queries — or just one? Walk the trade.

start.text: A 100,000-row list needs its first lookup, today, once.

choices.label: Put it in order (n log n), then halve every lookup
choices.feedback: Sorting costs n log n up front: for a list you will query once, that is a loss — scan and move on.

choices.label: Scan it linearly, top to bottom
choices.feedback: Up to n comparisons and it works on any order — for a one-off query, the honest bargain.

once.text: Found it. Tomorrow: ten thousand more lookups on the same list.

choices.label: Order it once now, halve forever after
choices.feedback: Query it many times and the prerequisite becomes a massive win — databases, dictionaries and every 'sorted by…' column exist for exactly this.

choices.label: Keep scanning each time
choices.feedback: n comparisons per query, ten thousand times — the unsorted habit stops scaling.

scanOk.text: Found. But tomorrow: ten thousand more lookups on the same list.

choices.label: Order it once now, halve forever after
choices.feedback: Query it many times and the prerequisite becomes a massive win — databases, dictionaries and every 'sorted by…' column exist for exactly this.

choices.label: Keep scanning each time
choices.feedback: n comparisons per query, ten thousand times — the unsorted habit stops scaling.

many.text: Ordered once, logarithmic forever — the prerequisite paid for many times over.

grind.text: Simple and correct — until the query count grows; then the question becomes how many lookups tomorrow brings.

config.why: Sorting costs n log n once; the halving method pays only when the list will be queried many times.

activities.anchor: Big-O is growth rate, not milliseconds
activities.caption: true or false — reading a growth label honestly
activities.name: algBigOJudge

statements.s: For n = 20, an O(n²) algorithm does 400 operations and is instantly done.
statements.why: Small n hides everything: the quadratic is still cheap at twenty items.

statements.s: An O(n²) label means the algorithm is slow at every input size.
statements.why: The curves part company at scale — below about twenty items you can barely separate them.

statements.s: The notation measures wall-clock time in milliseconds.
statements.why: It names how cost scales, never a stopwatch reading.

statements.s: Thinking in curves before writing code is what decides which programs survive scale.
statements.why: That widening gap, not any single value, is the whole argument of the lesson.

activities.anchor: Professionals debug by hand-trace first, debugger second
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a traced max-finder
activities.name: algSeedSpot

config.prompt: A winter-temperatures max-finder was traced on paper — one line is wrong. Click it:
config.correction: Seed with an item of the data: max ← −8. Then −8 stays, −3 beats it, −5 does not — the answer is −3, the only honest maximum for all-negative input.
config.why: The table's job is to make the lying line visible: here the opening row poisoned every row after it.

activities.caption: bet before you read on — what ships anyway
activities.name: algShipPredict

config.q: It runs without crashing and passes every normal example you tried. What still ships?
choices: Boundary bugs — the empty list, the single item, the value one past the limit
Syntax errors — the compiler just missed them
Nothing: if normal data passes, the algorithm is correct
Only performance issues — the happy path settles everything else
config.why: Correct and incorrect programs agree on normal data; the empty list, the single item and the value one past the limit are where they split.

activities.caption: call the failure rate of the professionals
activities.name: algBentleyEst

config.prompt: Bentley's 1986 challenge: what share of professional programmers wrote a buggy binary search?
config.why: Around ninety in a hundred — usually off-by-one errors. Two decades on, Java's own standard library carried an overflow bug in (low + high) / 2; the fix became low + (high − low) / 2.
config.context: The idea is easy; the edges are where correctness lives.
